imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.t: The territory taken by the German Empire from France in 1871, governed directly from Berlin until it returned to France in 1918.
imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.o: By the Treaty of Frankfurt of 1871, which ended the Franco-Prussian War, France ceded Alsace and part of Lorraine, including Metz, to the new German Empire. Instead of joining an existing state, the region became a Reichsland, an imperial territory under the emperor's direct authority.
imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.r: The territory was governed by an imperial governor in Strasbourg; the first was Edwin von Manteuffel. Tens of thousands opted for French citizenship and left. Germany invested in Strasbourg's university and new imperial quarter. A constitution of 1911 created a regional parliament, but the Saverne Affair of 1913, when soldiers abused civilians, revealed lasting tensions.
imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.e: After Germany's defeat in November 1918, councils briefly proclaimed the Republic of Alsace-Lorraine before French troops entered. The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 returned the territory to France, where it still keeps some distinct local laws.

inca-empire.t: The largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, Tawantinsuyu stretched some 4,000 km along the Andes, linked by roads and run without money or writing.
inca-empire.o: Around 1438 the ruler of the Kingdom of Cusco, Pachacuti, defeated the Chanka Confederation and launched campaigns of conquest. His son Túpac Inca Yupanqui conquered the Kingdom of Chimor and lands from Ecuador to central Chile, and Huayna Capac extended rule to the north.
inca-empire.r: The Sapa Inca, believed to descend from the sun god Inti, ruled four quarters from Cusco. A road system of some 40,000 km, the Qhapaq Ñan, connected the empire with relay runners and storehouses. Labour tax called mita built terraces, temples and fortresses such as Sacsayhuamán and estates like Machu Picchu. Records were kept on knotted cords called khipus. Quechua was spread as the common language, and conquered peoples were resettled as mitmaq.
inca-empire.e: A civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa followed Huayna Capac's death from smallpox. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca and executed him in 1533. Resistance continued in the Neo-Inca State, while Quechua and Andean traditions survive today.

inancids.t: A small Turkmen beylik around Denizli (Ladik) in south-western Anatolia, visited by Ibn Battuta.
inancids.o: In the later 13th century, as the Sultanate of Rum weakened, Turkmen frontier warriors took Ladik, near ancient Laodicea, and the Lycus valley. A local dynasty took shape there under Mehmed Bey and later took its name from Inanc Bey.
inancids.r: Little is known of the beylik's government. It lay on the trade road through the Meander valley and produced cotton textiles embroidered with gold that Ibn Battuta admired when he visited Ladik around 1333, describing its ruler as generous. The beylik often depended on the stronger Germiyanids to the north.
inancids.e: Around 1368 the Germiyanids absorbed Ladik, and the region later passed with Germiyan lands to the Ottomans.

isle-of-man.t: A self-governing Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea, with one of the world's oldest continuous parliaments, the Tynwald.
isle-of-man.o: The British crown bought the sovereign rights of the Lordship of Mann from the Duke of Atholl through the Revestment Act of 1765, mainly to stop smuggling that cost the Treasury duties. The island became a direct possession of the crown, though not part of the United Kingdom.
isle-of-man.r: Man kept its own Tynwald, with the elected House of Keys and the Legislative Council, its own laws and taxes. It grew as a Victorian resort, with Douglas as capital from 1869, and hosted internment camps in both world wars. The TT motorcycle races began in 1907. The Manx language nearly died out in 1974 but is being revived.
isle-of-man.e: Since the mid 20th century the Isle of Man has expanded self-government and become an offshore financial centre. It remains a Crown Dependency, with the UK responsible for defence and foreign relations.

ilergetes.t: The leading Iberian people of the Lleida plain, whose chiefs Indibilis and Mandonius switched between Carthage and Rome in the Second Punic War.
ilergetes.o: The Ilergetes occupied the plains of the Segre and Cinca rivers around modern Lleida from the 5th century BCE, with their capital at Iltirta. By the late 3rd century BCE they were among the most powerful peoples of north-eastern Iberia.
ilergetes.r: They were ruled by princes who could raise large armies and dominate neighbouring peoples. Their economy rested on the cereal plains of the Segre, and Iltirta minted coins with an Iberian legend. During the Second Punic War their leaders Indibilis and Mandonius first served Carthage, then joined Scipio in 209 BCE.
ilergetes.e: In 206 and 205 BCE the brothers revolted against Rome; Indibilis died in battle and Mandonius was handed over and executed. The Ilergetes were absorbed into Hispania Citerior, and Iltirta became Roman Ilerda, where Caesar defeated Pompey's legates in 49 BCE.

italian-islands-of-the-aegean.t: Italy's Dodecanese colony, seized from the Ottomans in 1912, which left a legacy of Italian architecture before passing to Greece in 1947.
italian-islands-of-the-aegean.o: During the Italo-Turkish War of 1911-1912, Italy occupied Rhodes and the other islands of the Dodecanese. The Treaty of Ouchy in 1912 made the occupation provisional, but Italy kept the islands through the First World War, and the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 recognised its sovereignty.
italian-islands-of-the-aegean.r: Italian governors ruled from Rhodes. Mario Lago (1922-1936) invested in roads, agriculture, archaeology and buildings, including the restored Palace of the Grand Master and new Italian rationalist architecture. His successor Cesare Maria De Vecchi pursued forced Italianisation of education and the Orthodox church. Many Greeks emigrated.
italian-islands-of-the-aegean.e: After Italy's armistice in 1943 German troops took over, defeating the British at Leros and deporting the Jews of Rhodes in 1944. British military administration followed in 1945, and the Paris Peace Treaty of 1947 gave the islands to the Kingdom of Greece; they were formally united in 1948.

ilmen-slavs.t: The northernmost East Slavs, centred on Lake Ilmen, whose invitation to Rurik began the Rurikid dynasty in the chronicle tradition.
ilmen-slavs.o: Slavs reached the basin of Lake Ilmen and the Volkhov river in the 7th and 8th centuries, settling among Finnic and Baltic peoples. The chronicles call them the Slovene. Their main centres were the trading settlement of Staraya Ladoga and Rurikovo Gorodishche near the later Novgorod.
ilmen-slavs.r: They lived from farming, fishing, hunting and the fur trade, and their territory sat on the routes linking the Baltic with the Volga and the Dnieper. Scandinavian merchants and warriors were present from the 8th century. The tribe was led by elders and assemblies, which foreshadowed the later town assembly, the veche, of Novgorod.
ilmen-slavs.e: According to the Primary Chronicle, the Slovene, Krivichs and Finnic tribes expelled the Varangians and then invited Rurik to rule them in 862. In 882 his successor Oleg moved south to Kiev, and Ilmen became the northern half of Kievan Rus'. Their land developed into the Novgorod Republic.

imperial-abbey-of-weingarten.t: Benedictine abbey founded by the Guelphs that guarded a relic of the Holy Blood and built the largest baroque church in Germany.
imperial-abbey-of-weingarten.o: The Guelph family founded a convent at Altdorf near Ravensburg in the 11th century and in 1056 replaced it with a Benedictine abbey that became their family monastery. In 1094 Judith of Flanders, wife of Welf IV, gave it a relic of the Holy Blood. After the Guelph and Hohenstaufen lines passed, the abbey became imperial, by around 1274.
imperial-abbey-of-weingarten.r: The abbots ruled villages and farmland in Upper Swabia, sat among the Swabian imperial prelates and were among the richest in the region. The Holy Blood relic drew pilgrims, and the Blutritt horseback procession continues today. The Weingarten manuscript of medieval German love songs was kept there. From 1715 to 1724 the abbey built its vast baroque basilica.
imperial-abbey-of-weingarten.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803, passing to the house of Nassau-Orange and in 1806 to Württemberg. Benedictine monks returned in the 20th century, and the basilica remains a major pilgrimage church.

inner-austria.t: The Habsburg lands of Styria, Carinthia and Carniola, ruled from Graz, from which Ferdinand II launched the Counter-Reformation across the monarchy.
inner-austria.o: The Treaty of Neuberg of 1379 gave Leopold III the Habsburg lands south and west of Austria, including Styria, Carinthia and Carniola. These duchies were ruled as Inner Austria by Leopold's descendants in the 15th century; Frederick III, who resided at Graz and Wiener Neustadt, later reunited the dynasty's lands. In 1564 Ferdinand I's will recreated Inner Austria for his son Charles II.
inner-austria.r: From Graz the archdukes governed Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, Gorizia and Trieste with their own estates, which were largely Protestant in the 16th century. Inner Austria bore the brunt of Ottoman raids and paid for the Croatian and Slavonian Military Frontier. Charles II founded the University of Graz in 1585 under the Jesuits, and his son Ferdinand expelled Protestant preachers from 1598.
inner-austria.e: In 1619 Archduke Ferdinand became emperor as Ferdinand II, and his Inner Austrian lands merged into the united Habsburg Monarchy, though separate institutions in Graz survived until Maria Theresa's reforms in the 1740s.

indigetes.t: The Iberian people of the Empordà, neighbours of Greek Emporion, whose hill town at Ullastret is the largest Iberian site in Catalonia.
indigetes.o: The Indigetes occupied the Empordà plain of north-east Catalonia from about the 6th century BCE. Their growth was closely linked with the founding of Emporion by Greeks around 575 BCE, and part of their community lived beside the Greek town, which Livy describes as a double city.
indigetes.r: Their largest settlement, at Ullastret, was a walled hill town with towers, temples and grain silos, showing strong Greek influence in its architecture and imports. The Indigetes exchanged grain and other goods for Greek pottery and wine, and minted coins with the Iberian legend Untikesken. Their political organisation was probably based on town elites.
indigetes.e: They took part in the north-eastern revolt against Rome and were subdued by Cato in 195 BCE. Ullastret was abandoned soon afterwards, and the Indigetes merged with the population of Roman Emporiae and Hispania Citerior.

imamate-of-oman.t: The 20th-century Ibadi imamate of interior Oman, autonomous from the sultan of Muscat under the Treaty of Seeb until the Jebel Akhdar War.
imamate-of-oman.o: Interior tribes resented the coastal Sultanate of Muscat and Oman, its British ties and its curbs on the arms trade. In 1913 Ibadi scholars and tribal leaders elected Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi as imam at Tanuf; his forces took Nizwa and threatened Muscat, which was saved by British Indian troops.
imamate-of-oman.r: The imamate revived the old Ibadi ideal of an elected imam ruling by Islamic law, with Nizwa as capital and tribal leaders such as Isa ibn Salih al-Harthi as its strongmen. The Treaty of Seeb of 1920 gave the interior wide autonomy. Under Imam Muhammad al-Khalili, from 1920 to 1954, it remained isolated and conservative, with little trade or modern administration.
imamate-of-oman.e: After al-Khalili's death, Imam Ghalib ibn Ali sought outside recognition as oil exploration began. Sultan Said bin Taimur's forces, backed by Britain, occupied Nizwa in 1955, and the Jebel Akhdar War ended in 1959 when British troops stormed the mountain. The leaders went into exile.

isuwa.t: Isuwa, a Hurrian kingdom on the upper Euphrates, a buffer whose loyalty swung between the Hittites and Mitanni.
isuwa.o: Isuwa lay in the Elazığ plain, east of the Euphrates in eastern Anatolia, a region rich in copper. It emerged as a kingdom by the 15th century BCE, inhabited by Hurrian-speaking people in the borderland between the Hittite Empire and the Mitanni Empire.
isuwa.r: Little is known of its government beyond Hittite treaties. Isuwa sheltered refugees from Hittite lands and often sided with Mitanni. Salvage excavations before the Keban Dam flooded the plain uncovered fortified towns of the period.
isuwa.e: Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire conquered Isuwa in the 14th century BCE and made it a vassal. After the Hittite collapse c. 1200 BCE, the region passed to the kingdom of Melid.

isle-de-france.t: French Mauritius, a naval base and plantation colony that threatened British India until its capture in 1810.
isle-de-france.o: France claimed Mauritius, abandoned by Dutch Mauritius in 1710, in 1715 and renamed it Isle de France. Settlers arrived from Ile Bourbon in 1721, and under governor Mahe de La Bourdonnais from 1735 the colony was developed, with Port Louis built as a capital and naval harbour.
isle-de-france.r: Run first by the French East India Company and from 1767 by the crown, the colony relied on enslaved labour from Madagascar and Mozambique for sugar and food production. The intendant Pierre Poivre introduced spices and created the Pamplemousses garden. During wars with Britain, corsairs such as Robert Surcouf raided British shipping from Port Louis.
isle-de-france.e: British forces captured the island in 1810, and the Treaty of Paris of 1814 confirmed its cession along with the Seychelles. Renamed Mauritius, it kept French law and language, and gained independence in 1968.

italian-republic-1802-1805.t: Napoleon's Italian Republic, the first state to bear the name Italy, governed for him from Milan by Francesco Melzi d'Eril.
italian-republic-1802-1805.o: At the Consulta of Lyon in January 1802, Italian delegates of the Cisalpine Republic accepted a new constitution and elected Napoleon Bonaparte as president. The republic was renamed Italian, a symbolic step for supporters of national unity.
italian-republic-1802-1805.r: Napoleon ruled from Paris, while Vice-President Francesco Melzi d'Eril governed in Milan, building an efficient administration, reforming finances, introducing conscription and making a concordat with the papacy in 1803. Milan's departments and prefects followed the French model, and the republic's army fought in Napoleon's campaigns.
italian-republic-1802-1805.e: When Napoleon became emperor of the French, he turned the republic into the Kingdom of Italy (Napoleonic) in March 1805 and crowned himself king in Milan.

illyrian-kingdom.t: Kingdom of the Illyrians on the eastern Adriatic, ruled at its height by Agron and Queen Teuta, whose piracy provoked Rome's first wars across the Adriatic.
illyrian-kingdom.o: Illyrian kingdoms appear from about 400 BCE, when Bardylis built a power that defeated Macedon in 393 and 359 BCE. In the 3rd century BCE the Ardiaean dynasty under Agron united the coast from the Neretva to Epirus, with Scodra (Shkodër) and Rhizon (Risan) as royal seats.
illyrian-kingdom.r: Kings ruled through tribal chiefs and depended on a strong fleet of light lembi, used for war and for raiding Adriatic and Ionian shipping. Agron defeated the Aetolians in 231 BCE. Royal coins were struck at Scodra and Lissus. Greek cities such as Pharos and Issa lay on its edges.
illyrian-kingdom.e: Teuta's attacks on Italian traders led to the First Illyrian War in 229 BCE, and Demetrius of Pharos provoked a second in 219 BCE. In the Third Illyrian War of 168 BCE Rome captured King Gentius at Scodra and split the kingdom, which later became the province of Illyricum.

imperial-abbey-of-irsee.t: Benedictine abbey in the Allgäu that gained immediacy late and became known for its scholarship in science and mathematics.
imperial-abbey-of-irsee.o: Irsee Abbey was founded around 1182 by the margraves of Ronsberg as a Benedictine monastery near Kaufbeuren. Over the centuries the abbots expanded their rights, and in 1692 the abbey bought the jurisdiction and was recognised as an imperial abbey, immediate to the Empire.
imperial-abbey-of-irsee.r: The abbot ruled a small territory of villages as a prelate of the Empire, with a seat on the Swabian bench of prelates. The monks rebuilt the abbey in baroque style and maintained a school and a respected natural sciences cabinet; Ulrich Weiss, a monk of Irsee, was a noted philosopher and mathematician of the Catholic Enlightenment.
imperial-abbey-of-irsee.e: The abbey was secularised in 1802 and its lands given to the Electorate of Bavaria. The buildings later served as an asylum, whose patients were victims of Nazi euthanasia killings, and are now a conference centre.

imperial-abbey-of-engelberg.t: A Benedictine abbey in a high valley of central Switzerland that ruled the valley as a tiny state until 1798 and still flourishes today.
imperial-abbey-of-engelberg.o: Conrad of Sellenbüren founded the Benedictine abbey of Engelberg in 1120 in a remote valley below Mount Titlis, with monks from Muri. In 1124 Pope Calixtus II and Emperor Henry V confirmed its foundation and imperial protection, making it a free imperial abbey.
imperial-abbey-of-engelberg.r: The abbots ruled the Engelberg valley as lords, with rights of justice over its farmers. Under Abbot Frowin in the 12th century the abbey had a notable scriptorium. Engelberg was protected by the Swiss cantons of Lucerne, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Uri, and dairying and cheese provided its income.
imperial-abbey-of-engelberg.e: French invasion in 1798 ended the abbey's secular rule, and the valley was incorporated into the Helvetic Republic. In 1815 it joined the canton of Obwalden. The monastery survives as an active Benedictine community, and Engelberg is now a resort.

iberian-union.t: The 60 years in which Spain's Habsburg kings also ruled Portugal and its empire, bringing the whole Iberian Peninsula under one crown.
iberian-union.o: King Sebastian of Portugal died without heirs at Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578, and his successor, the elderly Cardinal Henry, died in 1580. Philip II of Spain pressed his claim, won the Battle of Alcântara and was recognised as Philip I of Portugal by the Cortes of Tomar in 1581.
iberian-union.r: It was a personal union: Portugal kept its own laws, Cortes, currency and colonial administration, governed by a viceroy and the Council of Portugal. But union drew Portugal into Spain's wars, and the Dutch attacked Portuguese Brazil, Africa and Asia. The Count-Duke of Olivares's plans for tax and military integration caused growing resentment.
iberian-union.e: On 1 December 1640 Portuguese nobles rose in Lisbon and proclaimed the Duke of Braganza as John IV. The Restoration War ended with Spanish recognition of Portuguese independence in the Treaty of Lisbon of 1668.

iverni.t: People of south-west Ireland named by Ptolemy, whose name is linked to the Érainn and to Ériu, the Irish name for Ireland itself.
iverni.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Iverni in the south-west of Ireland, around modern Cork, with a town called Ivernis and a river Iernus nearby. Their name is related to Ivernia or Hibernia, the classical name for the island, and to the Érainn, a population group prominent in the early genealogies of Munster.
iverni.r: Classical sources record nothing of their rulers or customs. Early Irish tradition remembers the Érainn as an ancient people of Munster, ancestors of groups such as the Corcu Loigde and the Corcu Duibne, who were powerful before the rise of the Eóganachta. The region has many ogham stones, the earliest Irish writing.
iverni.e: By the early medieval period the Érainn had been eclipsed by the Eóganachta, who built the Kingdom of Munster around Cashel. Érainn descendants such as the Corcu Loigde survived as subordinate kingdoms in west Cork.

ilansura.t: Ilansura, a small kingdom of the Khabur region best known for the unhappy marriage of King Haya-Sumu to two daughters of Zimri-Lim of Mari.
ilansura.o: Ilansura was a city of the Ida-Maras district in north-eastern Syria whose exact site has not been identified. It emerged as an independent kingdom after the death of Shamshi-Adad and the break-up of the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia in the 1770s BCE.
ilansura.r: Its king Haya-Sumu was a close ally of Zimri-Lim of Mari, who gave him his daughters Shimatum and Kirum in marriage. Kirum's letters to her father, complaining of humiliation by her sister and pleading to come home, are among the most personal documents of the Mari archive.
ilansura.e: After Mari was destroyed by the Babylonian Empire c. 1760 BCE, Ilansura disappears from the record.

iar-connacht.t: The O'Flaherty lordship of Connemara and western Galway, whose rulers' raids led Galway city to pray for deliverance 'from the ferocious O'Flahertys'.
iar-connacht.o: The O'Flahertys were originally kings of Muintir Murchada east of Lough Corrib. Driven westwards by the Anglo-Norman de Burghs in the 13th century, they established themselves in Iar Connacht, the land west of Lough Corrib including Connemara.
iar-connacht.r: The O'Flahertys ruled a rugged land of bogs, mountains and sea, raising cattle and fishing, and building tower houses such as Aughnanure. Their galleys, like those of Grace O'Malley, who married Donal O'Flaherty, controlled the coast. They were frequently at war with the merchant town of Galway.
iar-connacht.e: The Composition of Connacht in 1585 converted Gaelic lordship into English tenure, and Sir Murrough O'Flaherty submitted to the crown. The family lost most of its estates in the Cromwellian confiscations of the 1650s.

imperial-abbey-of-kornelimunster.t: A Carolingian abbey near Aachen, founded by Louis the Pious for the reformer Benedict of Aniane, which ruled a tiny imperial territory until 1802.
imperial-abbey-of-kornelimunster.o: In 814 Emperor Louis the Pious founded a monastery at Inda, near his palace at Aachen, for Benedict of Aniane, the leading reformer of Frankish monasticism. In 817 a council held at Aachen imposed the Benedictine Rule on all monasteries of the empire, with Inda as a model house.
imperial-abbey-of-kornelimunster.r: The abbey received relics of Pope Cornelius in 875, and the place became known as Kornelimünster. Its abbots were princes of the Empire ruling a small territory, the Münsterländchen, of a few villages. Relics presented to the faithful included textiles believed to be from the Passion of Christ, shown every seven years in the Aachen pilgrimage.
imperial-abbey-of-kornelimunster.e: The French annexed the area in 1794 and dissolved the abbey in 1802. The territory passed to Prussia in 1815. The former abbey buildings later housed a collection of modern art, and the church continues as a parish church.

imperial-abbey-of-elchingen.t: A Benedictine abbey above the Danube near Ulm whose abbots ruled a small territory, and which gave its name to Napoleon's battle of 1805.
imperial-abbey-of-elchingen.o: The abbey was founded on a hill above the Danube in the early 12th century by local nobles related to the Hohenstaufen and settled by Benedictine monks. The Free Imperial City of Ulm held its advocacy for long periods, and the abbey achieved full imperial status at the end of the 15th century.
imperial-abbey-of-elchingen.r: The abbot governed several villages as a member of the Swabian Circle and of the Swabian bench of prelates. Disputes with Ulm, whose Protestant territory surrounded the abbey, were frequent. Elchingen remained Catholic and in the 18th century rebuilt its church in late Baroque and early neoclassical style.
imperial-abbey-of-elchingen.e: The abbey was secularised in 1802 and given to Bavaria. On 14 October 1805 Marshal Ney defeated an Austrian force at the Battle of Elchingen during the Ulm campaign and was later made Duke of Elchingen. The abbey church survives in Oberelchingen.

imperial-abbey-of-thorn.t: A tiny principality on the Maas ruled by an abbess and her chapter of noble canonesses, an imperial estate for five centuries.
imperial-abbey-of-thorn.o: The abbey was founded around 990 by Count Ansfried, later bishop of Utrecht, and his wife Hilsondis, with their daughter Benedicta as first abbess. It became a house of secular canonesses drawn from high-born families, and the register dates its status as an immediate imperial territory, with the abbess a princess of the Holy Roman Empire, to 1292.
imperial-abbey-of-thorn.r: The princess-abbess ruled the village of Thorn and a few surrounding hamlets with her chapter of noble ladies, who were not bound by permanent vows and could leave to marry. The abbey kept its own courts and sent a representative to the imperial diet's Westphalian circle. Its white-painted village remains well preserved.
imperial-abbey-of-thorn.e: French revolutionary troops occupied the area in 1794 and the chapter fled; the principality was abolished and its lands annexed to France. The last abbess was Maria Kunigunde of Saxony. Thorn later became part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

italian-republic.t: Modern Italy, a democratic republic since the referendum of 1946 and a founding member of the European Communities and NATO.
italian-republic.o: On 2 June 1946 Italians voted in a referendum to abolish the monarchy of the Kingdom of Italy, and Enrico De Nicola became provisional head of state. A Constituent Assembly drafted a new constitution, which came into force on 1 January 1948.
italian-republic.r: Italy is a parliamentary republic with a president as head of state. Christian Democrat governments led by Alcide De Gasperi and his successors anchored it in NATO in 1949 and the European Economic Community, founded by the Treaty of Rome in 1957. The economic miracle of the 1950s and 1960s transformed the country, though it suffered political terrorism in the Years of Lead and a lasting gap between north and south.
italian-republic.e: The Tangentopoli corruption scandals of 1992 swept away the old party system. Italy adopted the euro in 1999 and remains a major European economy; Sergio Mattarella has been president since 2015.

imperial-abbey-of-salem.t: A wealthy Cistercian abbey near Lake Constance whose abbots ruled one of the largest monastic territories in Swabia.
imperial-abbey-of-salem.o: Salem was founded in 1137 by the knight Guntram of Adelsreute as a Cistercian house settled from Lucelle. It grew rapidly under Hohenstaufen protection, and in 1354 Charles IV confirmed its direct dependence on the empire. Its status was contested for centuries by Austria and others, but its abbots sat among the prelates of the Imperial Diet.
imperial-abbey-of-salem.r: The abbots ruled a compact territory of villages north of Lake Constance through their own courts and officials, making Salem one of the richest imperial abbeys in Swabia, with vineyards, granges and town houses in Konstanz and Überlingen. Its great Gothic minster dates from around 1300, and the Baroque abbey buildings were rebuilt after a fire in 1697.
imperial-abbey-of-salem.e: In 1802 and 1803 the abbey was secularised and granted to the margraves of Baden, who turned it into Salem Castle, still owned by the family. In 1920 Kurt Hahn and Prince Max of Baden founded the Schule Schloss Salem boarding school there.

iazyges.t: Sarmatian horse nomads who settled the plain between the Danube and Tisza and fought Marcus Aurelius before becoming Roman auxiliaries.
iazyges.o: The Iazyges were a Sarmatian people of the steppe north of the Black Sea. In the first half of the 1st century CE they moved west into the plain between the Danube and Tisza in modern Hungary and Serbia, wedging themselves between Roman Pannonia and the Kingdom of Dacia.
iazyges.r: They were mounted pastoralists led by kings and nobles, famed for armoured lancers. Rome alternately paid and fought them, using them against the Dacians. In the Marcomannic Wars they invaded Pannonia; after defeat on the frozen Danube, King Zanticus made peace with Marcus Aurelius in 175 CE and sent 8,000 cavalry, many of them posted to Britain.
iazyges.e: They remained a troublesome neighbour, fighting Constantine and Constantius II in the 4th century. The arrival of the Huns around 375 overwhelmed them, and they were absorbed into the Hunnic sphere and later peoples of the Carpathian basin.

ilercavones.t: The Iberian people of the lower Ebro around Tortosa, near whose town Hibera the Scipios defeated Hasdrubal Barca in 215 BCE.
ilercavones.o: The Ilercavones lived around the mouth and lower course of the Ebro, in southern Catalonia and northern Castellón, from about the 5th century BCE. Their position on the river made them a crossroads between the Iberian peoples of the north-east and those of Valencia.
ilercavones.r: Little is known of their government. Their towns included Hibera, near modern Tortosa, and they lived from farming, fishing and trade along the river and coast. They minted coins with Iberian legends, and later the Roman town of Dertosa issued coins naming Hibera Iulia Ilercavonia.
ilercavones.e: In 215 BCE the Scipio brothers defeated Hasdrubal Barca near Hibera, securing the Ebro for Rome. The Ilercavones were pacified by 197 BCE and absorbed into Hispania Citerior, with Dertosa becoming their main Roman town.

imperial-abbey-of-rot-an-der-rot.t: A Premonstratensian abbey in upper Swabia, the order's first house in the region, whose abbots ruled a small imperial territory.
imperial-abbey-of-rot-an-der-rot.o: Founded around 1126 by Premonstratensian canons, Rot was the first house of the order in Swabia. Its lands grew through gifts from local nobles, and in 1376 Emperor Charles IV confirmed its direct dependence on the empire, freeing it from outside advocates.
imperial-abbey-of-rot-an-der-rot.r: The abbot governed several villages in the Rot valley as a member of the Swabian Circle and of the Swabian bench of prelates in the Imperial Diet. The abbey's income came from farms, forests and tithes. It remained Catholic and in the 18th century rebuilt its church of Saint Verena in late Baroque style.
imperial-abbey-of-rot-an-der-rot.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and given to the counts of Wartenberg as compensation, and in 1806 it passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg. The church and abbey buildings survive in Rot an der Rot.

imperial-abbey-of-kaisheim.t: Wealthy Cistercian abbey near Donauwörth whose abbots won immediacy within the Empire and ruled villages across Swabia.
imperial-abbey-of-kaisheim.o: Kaisheim Abbey was founded in 1133 by Count Henry of Lechsgemünd and settled by Cistercian monks. It gained imperial protection early, but its status was disputed for centuries with the dukes of Bavaria and the counts of Oettingen, until its immediacy was recognised in 1656.
imperial-abbey-of-kaisheim.r: The abbot ruled as a prelate of the Empire, sitting on the Swabian bench of prelates in the Imperial Diet. The abbey held lands, villages and town houses around the Danube and Lech, collecting rents and tithes. It built a large baroque complex at Kaisheim and was known for its library and its imperial hall, the Kaisersaal.
imperial-abbey-of-kaisheim.e: In the secularisation of 1802 and 1803 the abbey was dissolved and its lands given to the Electorate of Bavaria. The buildings became a prison, which they still house today.

italian-governorate-of-montenegro.t: Italian-occupied Montenegro in the Second World War, where a planned puppet kingdom was swept away by one of the first mass uprisings in occupied Europe.
italian-governorate-of-montenegro.o: After the conquest of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in April 1941, Italy occupied Montenegro and planned to restore it as a separate state under Italian protection. On 12 July 1941 an assembly in Cetinje proclaimed the restoration of Montenegro's independence. The next day, 13 July, Communist-led Partisans and other insurgents launched a general uprising that liberated most of the country.
italian-governorate-of-montenegro.r: Italian forces reconquered the towns, and in October 1941 Montenegro was placed under a military governor, General Alessandro Pirzio Biroli, with harsh reprisals. The occupiers cooperated with Chetnik and separatist groups against the Partisans, and much of the mountainous interior remained a battleground between them.
italian-governorate-of-montenegro.e: When Italy capitulated in September 1943, German forces took over the occupation. The Partisans liberated Montenegro by December 1944, and it became a republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The 13 July uprising is a Montenegrin national holiday.

ialysos.t: One of the three ancient cities of Rhodes, on the hill of Philerimos, home of the famous Olympic boxing family of Diagoras.
ialysos.o: Ialysos lay on the north-west coast of Rhodes, below Mount Philerimos. A Minoan and then Mycenaean settlement flourished there, with rich chamber tombs. In the early Iron Age Dorian Greeks settled, and Ialysos became one of the three cities of Rhodes, with Lindos and Kamiros, in the Dorian Hexapolis.
ialysos.r: The city's acropolis sanctuary of Athena and Zeus Polieus stood on Philerimos. Ialysos took part in Rhodian trade and colonisation, and came under the Achaemenid Empire before joining the Delian League. Its leading family, the Diagorids, produced Olympic champions, including the boxer Diagoras, celebrated by Pindar in 464 BCE.
ialysos.e: In 408 BCE Ialysos joined Lindos and Kamiros to found the city of Rhodes, which absorbed its political life. Ialysos continued as a religious centre and later hosted a Byzantine fortress and a monastery of the Knights of Hospitaller Rhodes.

islamic-state-of-medina.t: The first Muslim community-state, founded by Muhammad at Medina in 622, which united most of Arabia within a decade.
islamic-state-of-medina.o: In 622 Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for Yathrib, later called Medina, at the invitation of its feuding Arab tribes. This migration, the Hijra, became the start of the Islamic calendar. The document known as the Constitution of Medina bound the emigrants, the local Muslims and the Jewish tribes into a single community, the umma.
islamic-state-of-medina.r: Muhammad acted as prophet, judge and military leader. Revelations of the Quran in this period set out rules on prayer, fasting, alms, marriage and inheritance. The community fought Pre-Islamic Mecca at Badr (624), Uhud (625) and the Trench (627), and expelled or defeated the Jewish tribes of Medina. The Treaty of Hudaybiyya in 628 brought a truce.
islamic-state-of-medina.e: Mecca surrendered in 630, and delegations from across Arabia submitted in the following two years. When Muhammad died in 632, Abu Bakr was chosen as his successor, founding the Rashidun Caliphate. Medina remained its capital and is the second holiest city of Islam.

imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.t: A Premonstratensian abbey in upper Swabia, famed for its rococo library hall, whose abbots ruled a small imperial territory.
imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.o: Founded in 1183 by the lords of Schussenried as a house of Premonstratensian canons, the community was raised to an abbey in 1440. Its abbots gradually freed themselves from outside advocates, gaining imperial immediacy and a seat among the Swabian prelates of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.r: The abbot ruled several villages in upper Swabia as a member of the Swabian Circle, supported by farms, forests and tithes. The abbey commissioned the pilgrimage church of Steinhausen, built by Dominikus Zimmermann from 1728, and in the 18th century began a grand new monastery whose library hall, painted by Franz Georg Hermann, is a masterpiece of rococo.
imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.e: Secularised in 1803, Schussenried was granted to the counts of Sternberg-Manderscheid and passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1806. The library hall survives in Bad Schussenried.

idumea.t: Small Livonian-Latgalian district in northern Latvia where the chronicler Henry of Livonia served as a parish priest.
idumea.o: Idumea lay north of the Gauja river, between the Liv lands of Turaida and Metsepole and the Latgalian land of Tālava. Its population was mixed Livonian and Latgalian, and it appears in Henry of Livonia's chronicle in the early 13th century.
idumea.r: Its people lived in small farming communities under local elders. After the Germans arrived they accepted baptism, and Henry himself, the author of the chronicle, was ordained and served as priest among the Idumeans from about 1208.
idumea.e: Idumea came under the bishop of Riga around 1206 and became part of the Archbishopric of Riga and Terra Mariana. Its people were absorbed into the Latvian population.
idumea.re: Baltic and Finnic paganism, later Christianity

insubres.t: Celtic people of the Po plain who founded Milan and were the strongest Gaulish opponents of Rome in northern Italy.
insubres.o: Livy says Celts led by Bellovesus crossed the Alps around 600 BCE and founded Mediolanum, the later Milan, on land already called Insubrian. Archaeology shows the local Golasecca culture, which already spoke a Celtic language, Lepontic, absorbing larger Gaulish migrations in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE.
insubres.r: The Insubres formed a tribal state with Mediolanum as a central place, ruled by warrior aristocrats and kings. They lived in villages and fortified centres, farmed the rich plain and minted silver coins imitating those of Massalia. They often led the Cisalpine Gauls in war, joining the Boii against Rome in 225 BCE.
insubres.e: Rome defeated them at Telamon in 225 BCE and at Clastidium in 222 BCE, and took Mediolanum. They backed Hannibal, but after defeats in 196 and 194 BCE they accepted a treaty. Their land was gradually Romanised, gaining Latin and then full citizenship in the 1st century BCE.

imperial-abbey-of-werden.t: A Benedictine abbey on the Ruhr founded by the missionary Saint Ludger, which ruled a small imperial territory for a thousand years.
imperial-abbey-of-werden.o: Saint Ludger, a Frisian missionary and later first bishop of Münster, founded a monastery at Werden on the Ruhr around 799 on land he had acquired. He was buried there in 809, and his family's abbots ran the house for decades. In 877 it became a royal abbey under imperial protection.
imperial-abbey-of-werden.r: Werden held estates from Frisia to the Rhineland, and its abbots ruled the area around Werden as princes of the Empire. Its library held the Codex Argenteus, the silver Bible of the Gothic language, before it passed to Prague and later Uppsala. The protectors of the abbey were the counts of the Mark and later the rulers of Brandenburg-Prussia.
imperial-abbey-of-werden.e: Werden remained a Catholic island but a small one. In 1803 the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss secularised it and gave it to Prussia. Its Romanesque church, the basilica of Saint Ludger, survives in what is now a district of Essen.

imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.t: A Premonstratensian abbey on the Danube in upper Swabia whose abbots ruled a small territory of villages until 1803.
imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.o: A collegiate foundation existed at Marchtal from the 8th century, and in 1171 Count Palatine Hugh of Tübingen refounded it for Premonstratensian canons. Raised to an abbey in 1440, it gained imperial immediacy around 1500, and its abbot sat on the Swabian bench of prelates.
imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.r: The abbot governed several villages along the Danube and in the hills nearby. Between 1686 and 1701 the canons built a large new church, designed by the Vorarlberg masters Michael and Christian Thumb, one of the earliest great Baroque churches of upper Swabia. The abbey remained Catholic.
imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and given to the princes of Thurn und Taxis, who used the buildings as a residence. The territory passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1806, and the former abbey now belongs to the diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart.

imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.t: An island abbey on Lake Constance and one of the great centres of Carolingian and Ottonian learning and book painting, now a World Heritage Site.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.o: In 724 the wandering bishop Pirmin founded a Benedictine monastery on the island of Reichenau in Lake Constance, with the support of Charles Martel. It quickly became one of the leading abbeys of the Frankish realm, receiving estates across Alamannia and close links with the Carolingian court.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.r: Reichenau flourished in the 9th to 11th centuries: Abbot Walafrid Strabo wrote his poem on gardening, the Hortulus, there; the abbey library was among the largest in Europe; and its scriptorium produced Ottonian illuminated manuscripts for emperors. Its abbots were imperial princes who ruled a small territory around the lake.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.e: The abbey declined from the 13th century as its income fell and its noble-only admissions shrank the community. In 1540 it was incorporated into the Prince-Bishopric of Constance, whose bishops became its abbots. It was secularised in 1803; its churches at Oberzell, Mittelzell and Niederzell survive.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.la: Latin, Old and Middle High German

ionian-league.t: Religious and political union of twelve Ionian cities on the coast of Anatolia, centred on the Panionion, which led the Ionian Revolt against Persia.
ionian-league.o: The twelve cities were Miletus, Myus, Priene, Ephesus, Colophon, Lebedos, Teos, Clazomenae, Phocaea, Samos, Chios and Erythrae; Smyrna joined later. They formed the league c. 700 BCE, after destroying the city of Melia, whose land became the site of the Panionion, a shrine of Poseidon Helikonios on Mount Mycale.
ionian-league.r: The league held the Panionia festival and met to discuss common affairs, but the cities stayed independent and often fought each other. Thales proposed a single council at Teos, and Bias of Priene urged mass emigration to Sardinia when Persia attacked c. 545 BCE; neither advice was followed. The cities fell to the Kingdom of Lydia and the Achaemenid Empire.
ionian-league.e: Delegates met at the Panionion to coordinate the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE, which ended with defeat at Lade and the sack of Miletus in 494 BCE. The league survived later only as a religious association.
ionian-league.re: Greek religion; cult of Poseidon Helikonios

imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.t: A noble women's convent founded by the ancestors of the Ottonian emperors, home of Hrotsvitha, the first known German woman poet and playwright.
imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.o: The Saxon count Liudolf and his wife Oda founded a convent in 852 at Brunshausen, which moved to Gandersheim in 856. Their daughter Hathumod was the first abbess. As the family monastery of the Liudolfings, who became the Ottonian kings, it enjoyed royal favour, and in 919 it was made a royal abbey.
imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.r: Gandersheim was a community of canonesses, mostly from high noble families, ruled by an abbess who became a princess of the Empire. Around 960 the canoness Hrotsvitha wrote Latin plays, legends and verse histories of Otto I there. The abbey ruled a small territory around Bad Gandersheim under the protection of the dukes of Brunswick.
imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.e: Gandersheim accepted the Reformation in the 1560s, becoming a Lutheran foundation under the Brunswick dukes. It lost its imperial status with secularisation in 1802 to 1803, passing to Brunswick, and the convent was dissolved in 1810 under the Kingdom of Westphalia.

ile-bourbon.t: France's Indian Ocean island colony of Bourbon, built on coffee, sugar and slavery, which became the department of Reunion in 1946.
ile-bourbon.o: France claimed the uninhabited island in 1642 and named it Bourbon after the royal house in 1649. Permanent settlement began in 1665 when the French East India Company sent Etienne Regnault as commandant with a small group of colonists, joined by survivors from the Fort-Dauphin Colony.
ile-bourbon.r: From 1715 the Company introduced coffee, and the island became a plantation society worked by enslaved people from Madagascar, Mozambique and India. Mahe de La Bourdonnais governed it together with Isle de France in the 1730s and 1740s. Renamed Reunion in 1793, the island was occupied by Britain from 1810 to 1815; sugar replaced coffee and slavery was abolished in 1848, followed by indentured labour.
ile-bourbon.e: Bourbon, by then known again as Reunion, remained a French colony until 1946, when it became an overseas department of France, a status it still holds.

imperial-abbey-of-prum.t: A great Carolingian abbey in the Eifel, the burial place of Emperor Lothair I and a rich imperial territory until Trier absorbed it.
imperial-abbey-of-prum.o: The abbey was founded in 721 by Bertrada the Elder, and refounded in 752 by her grandson Pippin the Short and his wife Bertrada of Laon, who gave it rich estates. Under Carolingian favour Prüm became one of the most important monasteries between the Rhine and the Meuse.
imperial-abbey-of-prum.r: The Prüm Urbar of 893, a register of estates and dues, is a key source on the Carolingian rural economy. Abbot Regino of Prüm wrote an important chronicle there, and Emperor Lothair I retired to the abbey and died there in 855. Later its abbot was a prince of the Empire ruling a small territory in the Eifel.
imperial-abbey-of-prum.e: Prüm's possessions shrank from the 13th century, and the archbishops of Trier sought control over it. In 1576 the abbey was incorporated into the Electorate of Trier, the archbishop acting as its administrator. The monastery itself survived until French secularisation in 1802.

italian-social-republic.t: The Fascist puppet state set up by Nazi Germany in northern Italy in 1943, with Mussolini at its head, which collapsed in April 1945.
italian-social-republic.o: After the Kingdom of Italy signed an armistice with the Allies in September 1943, German forces occupied northern and central Italy. German paratroopers freed Mussolini from captivity on the Gran Sasso, and he proclaimed a new Fascist state, with ministries scattered around Lake Garda, especially at Salò.
italian-social-republic.r: The republic depended entirely on German forces, who controlled the economy and deported Italian Jews and workers. Its Verona Manifesto of 1943 promised a socialist-style programme, and the Verona trial of January 1944 executed Galeazzo Ciano and others who had voted against Mussolini. Its militias and the Germans waged a bitter war against the partisan resistance, with reprisals against civilians.
italian-social-republic.e: The Allied offensive and a general partisan uprising in April 1945 brought collapse. Mussolini was captured while fleeing towards Switzerland and shot on 28 April 1945, and the German forces in Italy surrendered on 2 May.

imperial-abbey-of-essen.t: A royal convent for noble women whose princess-abbesses ruled the town of Essen and whose treasure includes the oldest surviving statue of the Virgin Mary.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.o: Essen Abbey was founded around 845 to 852 by Altfrid, later bishop of Hildesheim, as a community of canonesses for women of the Saxon nobility. It received royal protection and immunity, and under the Ottonians it became a favoured house of the ruling dynasty.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.r: The abbesses Mathilde, a granddaughter of Otto I, and Theophanu, granddaughter of Otto II, made Essen a centre of Ottonian art; the Golden Madonna of about 980 and the Otto-Mathilde Cross belong to its treasury. The abbess was a princess of the Empire with a seat in the Imperial Diet, and ruled the small territory around Essen, often in conflict with the town.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.e: Essen was secularised in 1803 and passed to Prussia; the last abbess was Maria Kunigunde of Saxony. The town grew into the centre of Ruhr industry, and the former abbey church became Essen Cathedral when the diocese was founded in 1958.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.la: Old Saxon, Middle Low German, Latin

ile-sainte-marie.t: An island off Madagascar's east coast that went from pirate haven to French outpost, ceded to France in 1750.
ile-sainte-marie.o: In the 1690s Ile Sainte-Marie (Nosy Boraha) became a base for pirates raiding the Indian Ocean, with a trading post run by Adam Baldridge supplying them. Descendants of the pirates and local Malagasy later formed part of the Betsimisaraka Confederation. In 1750 Princess Bety, daughter of Ratsimilaho, ceded the island to France.
ile-sainte-marie.r: The French East India Company established a small post, but disease and a Malagasy uprising soon forced its abandonment. France reoccupied the island in 1818 under Sylvain Roux, building at Ambodifotatra a base for trade and for French claims on Madagascar. It was administered from Ile Bourbon for much of the 19th century, with a small Catholic population.
ile-sainte-marie.e: In 1896 Sainte-Marie was attached to the new French colony of Madagascar, and it has been part of Madagascar since independence in 1960.

iraca.t: A Muisca priestly lordship centred on Sugamuxi, home of the great Temple of the Sun and chosen as the sacred heart of the Muisca world.
iraca.o: Iraca, centred on Sugamuxi, the modern Sogamoso in Boyacá, was one of the territories of the Muisca Confederation. Muisca tradition held that the culture hero Bochica, also called Idacansas, had lived there and named his successor before departing, making Sugamuxi a sacred place.
iraca.r: Iraca was ruled by a high priest, the iraca, who was chosen alternately from two local communities, Tobasá and Firavitoba, and confirmed by nearby chiefs. The Temple of the Sun at Sugamuxi drew pilgrims and offerings. Iraca stood apart from the rival zaque of Hunza and the zipa of Bacatá and was often allied with Tundama.
iraca.e: Spanish troops under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada reached Sugamuxi in 1537, and the Temple of the Sun burned down while soldiers looted it. Iraca was then absorbed into the New Kingdom of Granada. The temple has been reconstructed in Sogamoso's archaeological museum.

imperial-abbey-of-herford.t: A convent for noble women in Westphalia whose abbesses ruled as princesses of the Empire for a thousand years.
imperial-abbey-of-herford.o: Herford Abbey was founded around 789 by a Saxon noble named Waltger as a community of women, soon after Charlemagne's conquest of Saxony. Under Louis the Pious it became a royal abbey, and it was among the oldest women's foundations in Saxony. Queen Matilda, wife of Henry the Fowler, was educated there.
imperial-abbey-of-herford.r: Herford was a secular canonesses' foundation for daughters of the high nobility. Its abbess was a princess of the Empire with a seat in the Imperial Diet. The town of Herford grew around the abbey and joined the Hanseatic League. In the 17th century Princess Elisabeth of the Palatinate, correspondent of Descartes, was abbess.
imperial-abbey-of-herford.e: The town and abbey accepted the Reformation, the abbey becoming Lutheran, but its princely status remained under the protection of Brandenburg-Prussia. Herford's imperial status ended with secularisation in 1803, when its lands passed to Prussia. The convent was formally dissolved in 1810.

ireland.t: The sovereign Irish state established under the 1937 Constitution, which became a republic in 1949 and an EU member in 1973.
ireland.o: The Constitution of Ireland, drafted under Eamon de Valera and approved by referendum in 1937, replaced the Irish Free State with a state named Ireland, or Eire, with an elected President, Douglas Hyde being the first. It claimed the whole island but applied its laws to twenty-six counties.
ireland.r: Ireland stayed neutral in the Second World War and declared itself a republic in 1949, leaving the Commonwealth. It is a parliamentary democracy with the Oireachtas and a Taoiseach. Long dominated by the Catholic Church and emigration, it changed through economic openness, EEC membership in 1973 and the 'Celtic Tiger' boom of the 1990s.
ireland.e: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 replaced its territorial claim with an aspiration to unity by consent. Referendums legalised divorce, same-sex marriage in 2015 and abortion in 2018, and Ireland is a member of the eurozone.

icelandic-commonwealth.t: Medieval Iceland's kingless republic of chieftains and law assemblies, the society that produced the Icelandic sagas.
icelandic-commonwealth.o: Settlers, mostly from western Norway and the Norse colonies in the British Isles, occupied Iceland from about 870, a period recorded in the Landnámabók. Around 930 they founded the Althing, a general assembly at Þingvellir, which gave the island a common law without a king.
icelandic-commonwealth.r: Power rested with chieftains, the goðar, whose followers could choose which chieftain to support. A law-speaker recited the law at the Althing, and courts settled disputes, though there was no executive to enforce verdicts. In 1000 the Althing, guided by Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði, adopted Christianity. The Commonwealth produced the sagas, the Eddas and the histories of Snorri Sturluson.
icelandic-commonwealth.e: In the 13th century, the Sturlung Age, a few great families fought for supremacy, and the Norwegian king Haakon IV intervened. In 1262-1264 the Icelanders accepted the Old Covenant, submitting to Norwegian rule, and Gissur Þorvaldsson became earl. Iceland later passed to Denmark and regained independence as the Kingdom of Iceland and Republic of Iceland.

imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.t: Premonstratensian abbey near Ravensburg that ruled a small Swabian territory as an imperial prelacy and built a grand baroque church.
imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.o: The abbey was founded in 1145 by Gebizo of Ravensburg, a ministerial of the Guelphs, and settled by Premonstratensian canons. It lay on the Schussen just south of Ravensburg. With Hohenstaufen and later royal protection it gained imperial immediacy in the 13th century, around 1257.
imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.r: The abbots, elected by the canons, ruled villages, farms and forests around the abbey and sat on the bench of Swabian imperial prelates in the Imperial Diet. Their territory was small and rural, and they defended their rights against the Free Imperial City of Ravensburg and the Habsburg bailiwick. In the early 18th century the abbey rebuilt its church in baroque style.
imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and given to the counts of Sternberg-Manderscheid as compensation for lands lost to France, and in 1806 it passed to Württemberg. Its church survives as a parish church in Ravensburg.

imperial-abbey-of-murbach.t: A wealthy Alsatian abbey whose abbots were princes of the Empire, ruling a small Vosges territory until the French Revolution swept it away.
imperial-abbey-of-murbach.o: Murbach Abbey was founded in 727 in a valley of the southern Vosges by Saint Pirmin, with the support of the Alsatian duke Eberhard of the Etichonid family. It soon became one of the richest monasteries of Alsace, with estates stretching into Swabia and Switzerland, including the town of Lucerne, which it held until 1291.
imperial-abbey-of-murbach.r: The abbots became princes of the Holy Roman Empire, ruling Guebwiller and the surrounding valleys. Only nobles could join the community. In 1560 Murbach was united with the Abbey of Lure. After France gained Alsace in 1648, the princely abbots kept their rights under French sovereignty. The Romanesque abbey church still stands.
imperial-abbey-of-murbach.e: The monks, wearied by the remote valley, moved to Guebwiller, and in 1764 the abbey became a secular collegiate chapter. During the French Revolution in 1789 the chapter's lands were seized and its palaces in Guebwiller looted, ending more than a thousand years of ecclesiastical lordship.

itanos.t: Port city of far eastern Crete, involved in the founding of Cyrene and long locked in disputes over the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus.
itanos.o: Itanos lay on a bay at the north-east tip of Crete, near Cape Sideros, and was settled in the early Iron Age, possibly with Phoenician involvement. Herodotus tells that Corobius, a purple-fisher from Itanos, guided the Therans to Libya before they founded Cyrene c. 631 BCE.
itanos.r: Itanos lived from fishing, purple dye and trade, with coins showing sea creatures. It had a long-running dispute with Praisos and later Hierapytna over the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus at Palaikastro and the land around it. In the 3rd century BCE it hosted a Ptolemaic garrison, which protected it against its neighbours.
itanos.e: Rome arbitrated the Hierapytna dispute through Magnesia c. 112 BCE. Itanos was absorbed into Roman Crete after 67 BCE and was abandoned in the Byzantine period.
itanos.re: Greek religion; cult of Diktaean Zeus

imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.t: One of Bavaria's oldest Benedictine abbeys, which became an imperial principality of its own inside the walls of Regensburg.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.o: The abbey grew up in the 8th century over the tomb of Saint Emmeram, a Frankish bishop martyred around 652, and for long its abbots were also bishops of Regensburg. It separated from the bishopric in 975 under Saint Wolfgang. Its independence from Bavarian and episcopal control was confirmed by the king in 1295, and in 1731 its abbots were raised to princes of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.r: The prince-abbot sat in the Imperial Diet, which from 1663 met permanently in Regensburg, yet his territory was little more than the abbey precinct and a few estates. Saint Emmeram was famous for its scriptorium and library, which held the Codex Aureus of Saint Emmeram, and in the 18th century for scientific scholarship. It remained Catholic within a Lutheran free city, the Free Imperial City of Regensburg.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.e: In 1803 the abbey passed to the short-lived Principality of Regensburg under Karl Theodor von Dalberg and was dissolved; Regensburg went to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1810. In 1812 the buildings became the residence of the princes of Thurn und Taxis, who still live there.

ituraea.t: Ituraea, an Arab principality of the Beqaa valley and Mount Lebanon, known for its archers and its brigandage.
ituraea.o: The Ituraeans, an Arab people, took control of the Beqaa valley and parts of Mount Lebanon and the Hermon in the late 2nd century BCE, as the Seleucid Empire declined. Their ruler Ptolemy son of Mennaeus governed from Chalcis and extended power towards Damascus and the coast.
ituraea.r: Ituraean rulers were also high priests of a local cult, and their warriors were renowned archers later serving in Roman armies. Strabo describes them as brigands raiding the caravan routes. Ptolemy made peace with Pompey in 64 BCE and kept his principality as a Roman client.
ituraea.e: Ptolemy's son Lysanias was executed by Mark Antony in 36 BCE. Augustus took lands from the tetrarch Zenodorus and gave them to the Herodian Kingdom of Judea in 20 BCE, and Ituraea was divided among neighbours.

illyrian-provinces.t: French-ruled provinces on the Adriatic created by Napoleon, which brought modern administration and an early taste of South Slav unity.
illyrian-provinces.o: After defeating Austria, Napoleon took Carniola, western Carinthia, Gorizia, Trieste, Istria and Croatia south of the Sava under the Treaty of Schönbrunn in 1809. He joined them with Dalmatia, Ragusa and the Bay of Kotor, already in French hands, to form the Illyrian Provinces, cutting Austria off from the sea.
illyrian-provinces.r: A governor-general in Ljubljana, first Marshal Auguste de Marmont, ruled under French law, abolishing many feudal dues, building roads and opening schools teaching in Slovene and Croatian. The poet Valentin Vodnik celebrated the change in Illyria Revived. Conscription, heavy taxes and the Continental Blockade, which ruined Adriatic trade, made French rule unpopular.
illyrian-provinces.e: Austrian troops recovered the provinces in 1813, and they were formally dissolved in 1816, when most became the Kingdom of Illyria and Dalmatia a separate kingdom. The name Illyria inspired the Croatian Illyrian movement of the 1830s.

ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.t: A brief Ibadi revolt-state that rose in Hadramawt, took Sanaa, Mecca and Medina, and was destroyed by the last Umayyad caliph.
ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.o: In 746, as the Umayyad Caliphate was torn by civil war, the Kindite judge Abd Allah ibn Yahya, known as Talib al-Haqq, was proclaimed imam by Ibadi missionaries from Basra in Hadramawt. He quickly took Sanaa and became master of most of Yemen.
ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.r: The imamate followed Ibadi principles of an elected, accountable imam and avoided plunder and indiscriminate killing of opponents. In 747 his general Abu Hamza al-Mukhtar ibn Awf marched north, appeared at the pilgrimage, defeated an Umayyad army at Qudayd and occupied Mecca and Medina, where his sermons were long remembered.
ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.e: Marwan II sent Abd al-Malik ibn Atiyya with Syrian troops. He defeated Abu Hamza in the Hejaz in 747, then pursued Talib al-Haqq, who was killed in battle; by 748 Yemen was recovered. Ibadi activity continued in Hadramawt and inspired the First Ibadi Imamate of Oman.

italian-regency-of-carnaro.t: Poet Gabriele D'Annunzio's self-proclaimed state in Fiume, a theatrical experiment that foreshadowed the style and rituals of Italian Fascism.
italian-regency-of-carnaro.o: After the First World War, Italy and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia both claimed the port of Fiume, today Rijeka, which had an Italian-speaking majority in the town. On 12 September 1919 the nationalist poet Gabriele D'Annunzio led some 2,600 legionaries into Fiume and occupied it in defiance of the Italian government. In September 1920 he proclaimed the Italian Regency of Carnaro.
italian-regency-of-carnaro.r: Its constitution, the Charter of Carnaro, drafted with the syndicalist Alceste De Ambris, organised citizens into corporations and declared music a fundamental institution of the state. D'Annunzio's balcony speeches, uniforms, salutes and mass rituals were later copied by Mussolini. The town lived on smuggling and piracy while blockaded by Italy.
italian-regency-of-carnaro.e: The Treaty of Rapallo in November 1920 made Fiume a free state. When D'Annunzio refused to accept it, Italian troops and warships attacked in the 'Bloody Christmas' of December 1920, and he left in January 1921. The Free State of Fiume followed.

imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.t: A Premonstratensian abbey in Swabia whose abbots ruled a small imperial territory between Ulm and Augsburg.
imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.o: Roggenburg was founded in 1126 by the counts of Bibereck as a house of Premonstratensian canons. Raised to an abbey in 1444, it struggled for a century to free itself from outside advocates, and in 1544 its abbots won recognition of imperial immediacy.
imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.r: The abbot governed a compact territory of villages in the hills between the Iller and the Günz as a member of the Swabian Circle and the Swabian bench of prelates. Farming and forestry provided income. Between 1752 and 1758 the canons built a large rococo church, which still stands.
imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.e: In 1802 the abbey was secularised and annexed by Bavaria, and its library and treasures were dispersed. Premonstratensian canons returned in 1982, and Roggenburg is again a monastery.

iacetani.t: A Pyrenean people of the Jaca valley in Aragon, whose town Iaca is the ancestor of modern Jaca.
iacetani.o: The Iacetani lived in the upper valley of the Aragón river in the central Pyrenees, around modern Jaca, from at least the 5th century BCE. Their affiliation is uncertain: they may have been related to the Vascones or to the Iberian peoples to the south.
iacetani.r: Strabo places them in the foothills of the Pyrenees, and their town Iaca later minted coins with an Iberian legend. They lived from herding and farming in the mountain valleys. Nothing reliable is known of their rulers or institutions.
iacetani.e: They appear among the peoples subdued during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE, though the reference is disputed. Later they lay within Hispania Citerior, and during the Sertorian war their region was fought over; Iaca survived as a Roman town and gave its name to Jaca.

imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.t: A convent founded at the tomb of King Henry the Fowler, whose princess-abbesses, often royal women, ruled Quedlinburg for nearly nine centuries.
imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.o: After King Henry the Fowler died in 936 and was buried at Quedlinburg, his widow Matilda and their son Otto I founded a community of canonesses there to pray for him. Otto's daughter Matilda became its first abbess in 966, and during the minority of Otto III she acted as regent in Germany.
imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.r: Quedlinburg was a favoured Ottonian palace where emperors celebrated Easter, and its abbesses were princesses of the Empire ruling the town and surrounding lands. The treasure includes Ottonian manuscripts and reliquaries, some stolen in 1945 and recovered in 1993. Abbess Anna II introduced the Reformation in 1539, and later abbesses were Lutheran princesses, often of the Swedish or Prussian royal houses.
imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and passed to Prussia. Its last abbess was Sophia Albertina of Sweden. The collegiate church and castle hill, with Henry's tomb, are part of the Quedlinburg World Heritage Site.

inalids.t: A Turkmen dynasty that ruled the walled city of Amid (Diyarbakir) for most of the 12th century after the fall of the Marwanids.
inalids.o: After the Seljuks ended the Marwanid emirate in the 1080s, a Turkmen commander named Inal established himself in Amid in the 1090s, founding a small hereditary emirate on the upper Tigris.
inalids.r: The Inalids held little more than Amid and its district and relied on alliances with the Artuqids and the Zengids. For long periods real power lay with their viziers of the Nisanid family, local notables who managed the city. Inscriptions on the great basalt walls of Amid record building work in this period. The population included Kurds, Arabs, Armenians and Syriac Christians.
inalids.e: In 1183 Saladin besieged and took Amid and handed it to his ally, the Artuqid Nur al-Din Muhammad, merging it into the Artuqids of Hasankeyf.

imperial-abbey-of-buchau.t: A house of noble canonesses on the Federsee whose princess-abbesses ruled a small territory of the Holy Roman Empire.
imperial-abbey-of-buchau.o: Tradition credits the founding of the abbey around 770 to Adelindis, a noblewoman linked to the Carolingians, on an island in the Federsee in upper Swabia. It became a house of secular canonesses drawn only from the high nobility. Its status under the emperor was confirmed in the 14th century, and its abbess came to rank as a princess of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-buchau.r: The princess-abbess sat on the Swabian bench of prelates in the Imperial Diet and governed villages around the lake and estates elsewhere. The canonesses took no permanent vows and could leave to marry. The neighbouring Free Imperial City of Buchau quarrelled with the abbey over rights for centuries. The house remained Catholic.
imperial-abbey-of-buchau.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and, with the town, granted to the princes of Thurn und Taxis as compensation for lost lands. In 1806 the territory passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg. The abbey church of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian survives in Bad Buchau.

iskolat.t: Soviet government of unoccupied Latvia in 1917-1918, backed by the Latvian Riflemen, the first Latvian soviet state.
iskolat.o: After the Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd in November 1917, Latvian Bolsheviks, strongly supported by the Latvian Riflemen, formed the Executive Committee of the Soviet of Workers, Soldiers and Landless of Latvia, known by its Russian acronym Iskolat. It governed the part of Latvia not occupied by Germany, with its seat in Valka and later Cēsis.
iskolat.r: Iskolat declared the land of the Baltic German manors nationalised, introduced eight-hour working days and organised local soviets. It worked closely with Lenin's government in Petrograd but had little time to build institutions, and Latvian nationalists rejected it as illegitimate.
iskolat.e: In February 1918 the German army advanced in Operation Faustschlag and occupied all of Latvia, and Iskolat fled to Russia. Its leaders later formed the Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic in December 1918, while nationalists proclaimed the Republic of Latvia.

idrisid-emirate-of-asir.t: A Sufi-led emirate on the Red Sea coast of Arabia that rebelled against the Ottomans, allied with Italy and Britain, and was absorbed by Saudi Arabia.
idrisid-emirate-of-asir.o: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi, great-grandson of the Moroccan Sufi teacher Ahmad ibn Idris, settled at Sabya in the coastal Tihama of Asir. Building on his religious prestige, he rallied the tribes against the Ottoman Empire's Yemen Vilayet around 1906-1910 and established an independent emirate.
idrisid-emirate-of-asir.r: The Idrisi ruled as a religious reformer and tribal leader, enforcing Islamic law and suppressing feuds. During the Italo-Turkish War Italy supplied him with arms, and in 1915 he signed a treaty with Britain against the Ottomans. After the war Britain handed him the port of Hodeidah in 1921, putting him at odds with Imam Yahya's Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen.
idrisid-emirate-of-asir.e: After Muhammad's death in 1923, succession quarrels weakened the emirate and Yahya took Hodeidah. In 1926 Hasan al-Idrisi accepted a Saudi protectorate; Ibn Saud annexed the territory in 1930, and after a failed revolt and the Saudi-Yemeni war of 1934 it was absorbed into Saudi Arabia.

independent-state-of-croatia.t: Axis puppet state ruled by Ante Pavelić's Ustaše, notorious for genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma during the Second World War.
independent-state-of-croatia.o: As German forces invaded the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, the Ustaše leader Slavko Kvaternik proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia in Zagreb on 10 April 1941, ending the Banovina of Croatia. Ante Pavelić returned from Italy as Poglavnik. The state included Croatia and all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in the Rome Agreements of May 1941 ceded much of Dalmatia to Italy.
independent-state-of-croatia.r: The Ustaše regime was a one-party dictatorship under German and Italian protection, with a nominal king, the Italian Prince Aimone, as Tomislav II from 1941 to 1943. It pursued the murder, expulsion and forced conversion of Serbs and the extermination of Jews and Roma, in camps such as Jasenovac. Much of its territory was contested by Partisans and Chetniks.
independent-state-of-croatia.e: As Partisan forces advanced, the state collapsed in May 1945. Its troops and civilians fleeing to Austria were turned back at Bleiburg and many were killed by the Partisans. Pavelić escaped to Argentina. The territory became part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.t: Benedictine abbey famed for its early medieval library whose prince-abbots ruled north-eastern Switzerland until the French invasion of 1798.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.o: The abbey grew from the cell of the Irish monk Gallus and was founded as a monastery by Otmar in 719. Its scriptorium, library and the Plan of Saint Gall made it a centre of Carolingian learning. Its abbots gained wide estates, and from 1206 they were recognised as princes of the Empire.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.r: The prince-abbots governed lands around Lake Constance and the Thur, but lost Appenzell in the Appenzell Wars and clashed with the city of St. Gallen. Abbot Ulrich Rösch rebuilt their power, buying the County of Toggenburg in 1468 and allying with the Old Swiss Confederacy. The abbey remained Catholic, while the city and parts of Toggenburg turned Protestant. Its baroque church and library were built in the 1750s and 1760s.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.e: The French invasion of 1798 and the Helvetic Republic ended its secular rule, and the abbey was dissolved in 1805. Its lands became the canton of St. Gallen in 1803. The abbey precinct and library are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

idel-ural-state.t: A Tatar-Bashkir national state proclaimed on the Volga in 1918 and suppressed by the Bolsheviks within weeks.
idel-ural-state.o: After the February Revolution, Muslim congresses in Kazan and Ufa debated autonomy for the Turkic peoples of the Volga and Urals. In late 1917 the National Assembly of Muslims of Inner Russia and Siberia resolved to create the Idel-Ural State, uniting Tatars, Bashkirs and Chuvash, with Kazan as capital, and its proclamation was planned for March 1918.
idel-ural-state.r: The project was led by Tatar politicians such as Sadri Maqsudi and Galimjan Sharaf, envisaging a democratic federal state with Muslim institutions and minority rights. It had a militia based in the Tatar quarter of Kazan, across the Bulaq canal, known as the 'Zabulachnaya Republic', but almost no administration beyond the city.
idel-ural-state.e: Bolshevik forces arrested its leaders in Kazan in February 1918 and dispersed the defenders of the Tatar quarter in March, ending the state. The Soviets later created the Tatar ASSR in 1920. The Idel-Ural idea survived among Tatar émigrés.

imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.t: Benedictine abbey on the Swabian Jura that bought its freedom from Württemberg and built one of Germany's great baroque churches.
imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.o: Zwiefalten was founded in 1089 by the counts of Achalm as a Benedictine monastery, settled from Hirsau. For centuries the dukes of Württemberg held its advocacy and pressed claims over it, until the abbey bought its independence in 1750 and became an imperial abbey.
imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.r: The abbot ruled several villages as a prelate of the Empire and sat on the Swabian bench of prelates. Wealth from estates paid for the rebuilding of the abbey church between 1739 and 1765 by Johann Michael Fischer, with stucco by Johann Michael Feichtmayr and frescoes by Franz Joseph Spiegler, a masterpiece of the late baroque.
imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.e: In 1802 and 1803 the abbey was secularised and its lands given to the Duchy of Württemberg. The monastery buildings became a psychiatric hospital in 1812, a role they still fill; the church is now a parish church.
