imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.t: A royal Carolingian abbey near Worms, famous for its gatehouse, its library and the Lorsch Codex, a vast record of medieval land grants.
imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.o: Lorsch was founded in 764 by the Frankish count Cancor and his mother Williswinda, and handed to Archbishop Chrodegang of Metz. Relics of the Roman martyr Saint Nazarius drew pilgrims and gifts. In 772 Charlemagne made it a royal abbey, giving it imperial protection and immunity.
imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.r: Lorsch grew into one of the richest abbeys of the Frankish realm, with thousands of donations recorded in the 12th-century Lorsch Codex. Its library held important classical and Christian manuscripts, and the Lorsch Pharmacopoeia is a key early medical text. The East Frankish king Louis the German and his son Louis the Younger were buried there.
imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.e: Decline came in the 12th century with disputes over its lands. In 1232 Emperor Frederick II gave Lorsch to the Archbishop of Mainz, ending its independence; the Electoral Palatinate later took control. Its gatehouse, the Königshalle, survives and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.t: One of the oldest and richest abbeys of the Rhineland, outside Trier, whose long fight to stay independent of the archbishops ended in 1669.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.o: Saint Maximin's Abbey grew around the tomb of Bishop Maximin of Trier in the 4th century and became a Benedictine abbey. It was richly endowed by Frankish kings and became an imperial abbey. In 1139 King Conrad III placed it under the Archbishop of Trier, beginning centuries of dispute over its status.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.r: The abbey held extensive estates in the Moselle region and Luxembourg and was a centre of the 10th-century Gorze reform movement. Its abbots claimed to be princes of the Empire with lands of their own, while the archbishops of Trier claimed the abbey as their territory, fighting the case in imperial courts.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.e: In 1669 the Imperial Aulic Council confirmed the Archbishop of Trier's lordship, ending the abbey's claim to independence. The abbey was dissolved under French rule in 1802; its rebuilt church survives in Trier as a school and event hall.

iceni.t: East Anglian kingdom whose queen Boudica led the great revolt of 60 or 61, burning Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before Rome crushed the rising.
iceni.o: The Iceni held Norfolk and parts of Suffolk and Cambridgeshire; they are probably the Cenimagni who surrendered to Julius Caesar in 54 BCE. In the 1st century BCE their elite deposited spectacular gold torcs at Snettisham, and from about 10 BCE they issued silver coins, some inscribed ECEN, with horse designs.
iceni.r: Coins name rulers such as Antedios, and settlements like Thetford and Saham Toney appear to have been major centres. After the Roman conquest of 43 the Iceni became a client kingdom, but they rebelled in 47 when the governor Ostorius Scapula tried to disarm them. Prasutagus later ruled as a client king, enjoying Roman favour while keeping horse-rearing and an independent elite.
iceni.e: When Prasutagus died around 60, leaving half his realm to Nero, Roman officials seized it, flogged his widow Boudica and raped her daughters. Boudica led the Iceni and Trinovantes in revolt and destroyed three cities before Suetonius Paulinus defeated her. The territory was annexed and later organised as a civitas centred on Venta Icenorum.

iapydes.t: Warlike people of the Lika and Una highlands in modern Croatia and Bosnia, blending Illyrian and Celtic culture until Octavian crushed them.
iapydes.o: The Iapydes formed in the hinterland of the northern Adriatic during the Iron Age, around the 6th century BCE, in the Lika plateau and the Una valley near Bihać. Their material culture developed from local Bronze Age traditions, with growing Celtic influence from the 4th century BCE.
iapydes.r: They lived in hillforts led by local chiefs, with Metulum as their main stronghold. They are known for stone cinerary urns carved with reliefs, distinctive bronze headgear and amber jewellery. Herding and raiding into the Roman province of Italy and on Aquileia brought them into conflict with Rome; a campaign under Sempronius Tuditanus defeated them in 129 BCE.
iapydes.e: In 35 BCE Octavian led his Illyrian campaign against them; at the siege of Metulum he was wounded and the defenders burned their town rather than surrender. The Iapydes were subdued by 34 BCE and absorbed into the province of Illyricum.

italiote-league.t: Alliance of the Greek cities of southern Italy against the Lucanians and the tyrants of Syracuse, later led by Taras until the Roman conquest.
italiote-league.o: The Greek cities of southern Italy, the Italiotes, drew together in the late 5th century BCE as Oscan-speaking Lucanians pressed on their territory and Syracuse grew ambitious. The Achaean cities, led by Croton, formed the core, with a common sanctuary at the temple of Hera Lacinia near Croton.
italiote-league.r: Members pledged to help any city attacked by the Lucanians, and the league had a common treasury and federal meetings. Its army was defeated by the Lucanians near Laus in 389 BCE and, in the same year, by Dionysius I at the Elleporus river, after which he dismantled Kaulonia and Hipponion. In the mid-4th century BCE Taras took the lead and moved the league's seat to Heraclea, hiring generals from Greece.
italiote-league.e: Under Tarentine leadership the league drew in Pyrrhus against Rome in 280 BCE. After his departure and the surrender of Taras in 272 BCE, the Greek cities became separate allies of Rome and the league ceased to exist.

imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.t: A wealthy Benedictine abbey in upper Swabia that broke free of Saint Blasien and ruled one of the largest monastic territories in the region.
imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.o: Founded around 1090 as a priory of the Black Forest abbey of Saint Blasien, Ochsenhausen became an independent abbey in 1391. In 1495 it was freed from outside advocates and recognised as an imperial abbey, with its abbot sitting among the Swabian prelates of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.r: The abbot ruled several dozen villages, making Ochsenhausen one of the largest monastic territories in Swabia. Its peasants rose against the abbey in 1502 and again in the Peasants' War of 1525. In the 18th century the monks rebuilt their church and buildings in Baroque style, and Joseph Gabler built a celebrated organ for the church in the 1720s and 1730s.
imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and given to Count Franz Georg von Metternich, father of the Austrian chancellor, as compensation for lands lost west of the Rhine. It passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1806, and the Metternichs sold their rights there in 1825.

imperial-abbey-of-lindau.t: A house of noble canonesses on an island in Lake Constance whose princess-abbesses ruled a tiny territory beside the free city of Lindau.
imperial-abbey-of-lindau.o: The women's community on the island of Lindau was founded in the 9th century, and the town that grew up beside it became a free imperial city. The abbey's direct dependence on the empire was confirmed in the 15th century, and its abbess ranked as a princess of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-lindau.r: The canonesses were noblewomen who lived without permanent vows. The princess-abbess governed scattered villages and rights around Lake Constance, but the abbey was entangled in long disputes with the city of Lindau, which adopted the Reformation in the 1520s, while the abbey remained Catholic.
imperial-abbey-of-lindau.e: In 1802 and 1803 the abbey was secularised and granted to the princes of Bretzenheim, who soon exchanged it; it passed to Austria and in 1805 to the Kingdom of Bavaria. The former abbey buildings stand in Lindau's old town.

imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.t: A Benedictine abbey in the Swabian Allgäu, founded in 764, whose abbots ruled a small territory and built one of Germany's grandest Baroque churches.
imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.o: Founded in 764 by the Swabian noble Silach and protected by Charlemagne, the abbey built up lands in the Günz valley. From the 13th century the prince-bishops of Augsburg held its advocacy, and the abbots spent centuries asserting their independence; only in 1710 did the abbey buy out Augsburg's rights and secure full imperial immediacy.
imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.r: The abbot ruled several villages as a member of the Swabian Circle and of the prelates' bench of the Imperial Diet. Income from farms, forests and tithes paid for learning and building: from 1711 Abbot Rupert Ness rebuilt the monastery, and under Anselm Erb the great church was completed to designs by Johann Michael Fischer, a masterpiece of south German Baroque.
imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.e: The abbey was secularised in 1802 and its territory annexed by the Electorate of Bavaria. Monks returned in 1834, and Ottobeuren is again a Benedictine community whose basilica and organs draw many visitors.

imperial-city-of-besancon.t: A free city of the Holy Roman Empire inside Franche-Comté, ruled by its citizens rather than its archbishops until Louis XIV took it in 1674.
imperial-city-of-besancon.o: Besançon was an ancient archbishopric whose archbishops long held authority in the city. After repeated revolts, the citizens obtained recognition of their liberties, and in 1290 Rudolf of Habsburg confirmed the city as a free imperial city, separate from the surrounding Free County of Burgundy.
imperial-city-of-besancon.r: The city was governed by elected governors and councillors drawn from its wards, while the archbishop kept spiritual and some ceremonial rights. It traded across the Jura and the Saône valley. In the 16th century Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, chancellor of Charles V, built his palace there, and the city was closely tied to the Habsburgs.
imperial-city-of-besancon.e: In 1654 the emperor ceded Besançon to Spain, joining it to Franche-Comté. Louis XIV took the city in 1674, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678 made it French. It became the capital of Franche-Comté, and Vauban built its citadel.

irish-free-state.t: The self-governing dominion of twenty-six Irish counties established by the Anglo-Irish Treaty in 1922, the forerunner of modern Ireland.
irish-free-state.o: The Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 created the Irish Free State as a dominion of the British Commonwealth, with the British monarch as head of state and an oath of fidelity. It came into being on 6 December 1922, during the civil war between pro-Treaty and anti-Treaty republicans.
irish-free-state.r: The Free State's first government under W. T. Cosgrave won the civil war in 1923, built a civil service, an unarmed police force, the Garda Siochana, and the Shannon hydroelectric scheme. It joined the League of Nations in 1923. Eamon de Valera's Fianna Fail took power in 1932 and dismantled Treaty links, removing the oath and fighting an economic war with Britain.
irish-free-state.e: A new constitution, approved by referendum in 1937, replaced the Free State with Ireland, or Eire.

italia-social-war-confederation.t: Rebel state formed by Rome's Italian allies in the Social War of 91–88 BCE, with its own capital, senate, consuls and coinage.
italia-social-war-confederation.o: For two centuries Rome's Italian allies supplied soldiers for its wars without full citizenship. When the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus, who proposed giving it to them, was murdered in 91 BCE, the Marsi, Paeligni, Samnites, Picentes and other peoples rose in revolt, starting with a massacre of Romans at Asculum.
italia-social-war-confederation.r: The rebels set up a federal state modelled on Rome, with Corfinium as its capital, renamed Italia, a senate of 500 members and two consuls, the Marsian Quintus Poppaedius Silo and the Samnite Gaius Papius Mutilus. They minted silver coins, some inscribed in Oscan as Víteliú, showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf. Their armies, trained in Roman methods, fought Rome on equal terms in 90 BCE.
italia-social-war-confederation.e: Rome divided the rebels by granting citizenship to loyal allies in 90 BCE and to all who laid down arms in 89 BCE. Sulla, Pompeius Strabo and Marius defeated the remaining forces, and Silo was killed in 88 BCE. Within a generation all free Italians south of the Po were Roman citizens.

irish-republic.t: The revolutionary republic declared in 1916 and established by Dail Eireann in 1919, which fought the War of Independence against British rule.
irish-republic.o: The Easter Rising of 1916 proclaimed an Irish Republic. After Sinn Fein won most Irish seats in the 1918 general election, its members met in Dublin on 21 January 1919 as Dail Eireann, adopted a Declaration of Independence and created a government, with Eamon de Valera as president from April 1919.
irish-republic.r: The republic built a counter-state: Dail courts, a loan raised by Michael Collins, local councils and the Irish Republican Army, which fought the War of Independence against British forces from 1919 to 1921. It was recognised by no foreign government.
irish-republic.e: After the truce of July 1921, the Anglo-Irish Treaty, approved by the Dail in January 1922, replaced the republic with the Irish Free State, a dominion. The split over the Treaty led to the Irish Civil War.
